content:
A chartered accountant firm can have a full website in 2026, and the rules are wider than many partners remember. Under the Council Guidelines for Advertisement in ICAI's revised Code of Ethics (13th edition, applicable from 1 April 2026), a firm is free to create its own website in any format and may show its name, year of establishment, offices, partners and their areas of experience, staff, the nature of services, peer review status, articles and educational videos, a secure client document area and, with the client's permission, client names. What it still may not do is solicit: no testimonials, no fees, no "leading firm" language, no banner advertising on the site, no campaign asking people to visit it, and no pushing of information about services reserved for chartered accountants, such as audit and attestation. A website designer in Pune who builds for CA firms has to work inside those lines, and this guide sets out where they are.

It is written for partners of small and mid-sized Pune firms. We quote clause numbers so you can check each point. It is not ethics advice: where the text leaves a question open we say so, and ICAI's Ethical Standards Board (ESB) is the body to ask.

## What changed, and what is in force today

The governing provisions are Clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Clause (6) makes it professional misconduct for a member in practice to solicit clients or professional work "either directly or indirectly by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or by any other means". Clause (7) prohibits advertising professional attainments or services, with a proviso that a member in practice "may advertise through a write up, setting out the services provided by him or his firm and particulars of his firm subject to such guidelines as may be issued by the Council".

Those guidelines are the Council Guidelines for Advertisement, 2008, printed as Chapter 3 of Volume I of the Code of Ethics; the website rules are paragraph 3.3.

Three dated facts matter:

- **12 December 2025:** ICAI's press release announced that the Council, at its 447th meeting, had approved the revised 13th edition of the Code of Ethics, including amendments to the advertisement and website guidelines. It said members and firms may use push technology for services not exclusive to the profession and that ICAI-registered network firms may have their own websites.
- **1 April 2026:** the revised Code became applicable.
- **30 May 2026:** the Ethical Standards Board published a notice with the three volumes and confirmed the 1 April 2026 applicability, with one exception unrelated to websites.

This article is based on that Volume I as downloaded on 18 November 2026. We found no later amendment to Chapter 3, but confirm on icai.org before you sign off content.

One loose end. On 14 October 2020 ICAI issued an advisory listing 29 contents and features prohibited on members' and firms' websites. Several items conflict with the revised text: the advisory bars client names, event photo galleries and any website running on a push model, while the 2026 text permits client names with permission, a gallery of professional events and push technology for non-exclusive services. TODO (verify): we could not find an ICAI notice saying whether the 2020 advisory has been withdrawn or reissued. Until that is clear, treat the items the revised Code does not contradict ("why choose us" blocks, "leading firm" claims, ISO badges, media coverage, empanelment lists) as still prohibited.

## What a firm website may and may not show

Clause numbers refer to Chapter 3 of Volume I of the Code, 13th edition.

| Item | Position | Clause |
|---|---|---|
| Firm name, year of establishment, offices, contact details, peer review status | Permitted | 3.3.7 |
| Nature of services | Permitted; exclusive services only on a "pull" request | 3.3.7 |
| Partners and employees: names, qualifications, area of experience | Permitted | 3.3.7 |
| Client name and nature of assignment | With the client's permission | 3.3.7 |
| Fees charged | Not permitted, unless a regulator requires disclosure | 3.3.7 |
| Banner or other advertisements on the site | Not permitted | 3.3.16 |
| Testimonials or endorsements | Not permitted | 3.1.3(E) |
| Awards and accreditations | Only awards from governments or regulatory bodies | 3.1.3(F) |
| Monograms, catch words, exaggerated claims, comparisons | Not permitted | 3.1.3 |

### The "pull" model after the revision

Clause 3.3.3 now says websites "may run on 'Pull' as well as 'Push' technology", but for services exclusively reserved for chartered accountants only the pull model is permitted: the information is to be provided "only on the basis of specific 'pull' request". Clause 3.3.4 adds that such information must not be circulated by email or any other mode except on such a request. The Code's own example of exclusive services, in a 2016 guideline on tenders, is "audit and attestation services".

For a builder this splits the site in two. Audit and assurance pages are reference pages that a visitor finds and reads; they stay out of newsletters, WhatsApp broadcasts and social posts. Pages on non-exclusive work such as accounting and consultancy have more room, though "push" is not defined in the text we read, so do not assume it covers every promotional technique.

### Membership and registration numbers

The write-up list in clause 3.2.1 permits the Firm Registration Number with the Institute and, for each member, the membership number. The website list in clause 3.3.7 does not name them, and we found nothing in Chapter 3 that makes them mandatory on a website. Showing the FRN in the footer and membership numbers on partner profiles lets a visitor verify the firm. Clause 3.3.21 requires that the website not be at material variance with ICAI's records, so copy names, addresses and numbers from those records, not from an old brochure.

### Client names, logos and testimonials

- **Client names** may appear with the client's permission, along with the nature of the assignment. Where the assignment is an exclusive service such as statutory audit, only the name may be mentioned. Keep the permission in writing.
- **Client logos** are not in the permitted list, which speaks of the "name of the client", and the 2020 advisory expressly barred them. Show names as plain text unless the ESB confirms otherwise.
- **Testimonials** remain out. Clause 3.1.3(E) says a write-up "should not contain testimonials or endorsements concerning Member(s) or the fees charged". That rules out testimonial sliders, star ratings copied from Google and quoted praise.

### Awards and adjectives

Awards from Central or State Governments or regulatory bodies may be mentioned; other awards, rankings and accreditations may not. Catch words are barred by clause 3.1.3(G): "Chartered Accountants, Pune, established 1998" is a particular, while "Your trusted growth partner" is a catch phrase.

## Page structure for a CA firm site

A structure that fits clause 3.3.7 and works for visitors:

1. **Home.** Firm name with "Chartered Accountants", year of establishment, a factual line on what the firm does and where, and links onward. No slogan, no client counters.
2. **About the firm.** Constitution, number of partners and staff by category, peer review status, and network affiliation if registered with ICAI.
3. **Services.** One descriptive page per service line.
4. **Industries.** A factual list of sectors, consistent with the permitted "area of experience" and "nature of services".
5. **Partners and team.** Name with the prefix CA, year of qualification, other recognised qualifications, areas of experience, contact details, passport-style photograph and membership number. Elected positions held in ICAI's Central Council, Regional Councils or branches may be mentioned (clause 3.3.19).
6. **Offices.** Head office and branches as registered with the Institute, with working hours and a map.
7. **Knowledge.** Articles, professional updates and educational videos.
8. **Careers.** Vacancies and articleship openings, without expressions such as "a well-known firm" (clause 3.7.2).
9. **Client login, contact and privacy notice.**

Two smaller rules affect the build. The domain name should be as near as possible to the firm or member's name (clause 3.3.20), and outbound links should stay within clause 3.3.18: ICAI and its regional councils and branches, government departments, regulators and other professional bodies.

On photographs, clause 3.3.9 permits passport-style photographs and a gallery of professional events organised by the firm or where partners lectured.

## Wording that informs and does not solicit

Clause 3.3.14 is the test every page has to pass: the details on the website "should be so designed that it does not amount to soliciting client or professional work".

| Soliciting | Informing |
|---|---|
| "Pune's most trusted audit firm" | "Statutory audit under the Companies Act, 2013 for private and public companies" |
| "Why choose us" with five ticks | A paragraph on who handles which work |
| "Book your free consultation today" | "For enquiries, write to the office nearest to you" |

Working rules for the copywriter:

- Write service pages as explanations: what the service is, who must have it done, what documents and steps are involved, which partner handles it.
- No superlatives, comparisons, fees, free offers, or claims about speed or success.
- Buttons say "Send an enquiry", not "Get started now". No pop-ups or countdown timers.

Advocates face a similar discipline under a different rule; see our guide to [advocate and law firm websites under BCI Rule 36](/blog/website-designer-pune-advocate-law-firm-website-bci-rule-36-2026).

## Enquiry forms and client document upload

### Enquiry forms

Nothing in Chapter 3 prohibits a contact form. Clause 3.3.13 allows members and firms to give online advice to clients "who specifically request for the advice", free or paid, and a form is how such a request arrives. Keep it plain: name, phone or email, office, subject and message. Do not add enquirers to any mailing about audit or other exclusive services, since clause 3.3.4 limits circulation of that information to a specific request.

Protect the form with a honeypot field, rate limiting and server-side validation, as described in our piece on [contact form spam and bot protection](/blog/website-designer-pune-contact-form-spam-bot-protection-2026).

### The client document area

Clause 3.3.11 says firms "can provide document management facility with distinct log in and password facility to the clients to access copies of their documents on the Firm website", and clause 3.3.15 says the website "should ensure adequate secrecy of the matters of the clients handled through Website". A careless upload feature is the largest risk on the site. A builder should follow the OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet:

- allow only the file types the firm needs and check the real type on the server, since the browser's content-type header can be spoofed;
- rename files on the server and store them outside the web root, never at a guessable public URL;
- set size limits and scan uploads for malware;
- restrict upload and download to authenticated users, each client seeing only their own folder.

Add two-factor login for staff, an access log, encrypted backups and session time-outs. If the firm already uses a practice management tool, linking to its login page is often safer and cheaper than building a second store of client files.

## Search visibility for a CA firm, as a website designer in Pune would plan it

### What the Code says about promotion

- Clause 3.3.5: chartered accountants must not issue "any circular or any other advertisement or any other material of any kind whatsoever by virtue of which they solicit people to visit their Website".
- Clause 3.3.16: no banner or other advertisement on the website itself.
- Clause 3.3.12: the firm may link to its social networking page but must not solicit people to visit or like it.

Read together, paid search and social advertisements that send people to the firm's website look hard to reconcile with clause 3.3.5, even after the push relaxation. TODO (verify): the Code does not mention paid search advertising by name, and secondary commentary is divided on whether the 2026 revision allows it for non-exclusive services. Get the ESB's view in writing before spending on ads.

### Organic search through useful articles

Unpaid search is a pull medium: a person asks a question and chooses a result. Clause 3.3.10 expressly permits "blogs, articles, professional information, bulletin boards, professional updation" on the website, which makes the knowledge section the firm's legitimate route to visibility.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks for people-first writing that shows expertise, with a higher standard for topics affecting a reader's financial stability. For a CA firm that means:

- articles written or reviewed by a named partner, with a byline linking to the partner's profile;
- a "last reviewed" date, because tax and company law content goes stale;
- the rule, who it affects and what to do, with the section cited, and no closing sales pitch.

One trap: the commentary under Clause (7) says educational videos, audios or podcasts uploaded on the internet should not contain the website address, though the firm name, address, phone and email may be mentioned.

Clean titles, fast pages, structured data that matches ICAI records and an XML sitemap are neutral plumbing; our [SEO service](/services/seo) for professional firms is limited to that plus editorial support for the knowledge section.

### Google Business Profile

Volume I does not mention Google Business Profile. The particulars a profile holds (name, registered address, working hours, phone, website) are all items the write-up list in clause 3.2.1 permits, so a plain, factual profile appears consistent with the Guidelines. TODO (verify): confirm with the ESB if your firm wants certainty. Keep to these limits:

- Use the exact firm name. Google's own guidelines forbid adding keywords, taglines or locations to the business name, which matches ICAI's rule against catch words.
- Do not run review campaigns, and do not reproduce Google reviews on the website: a review republished by the firm is a testimonial.

Our guide to [Google Business Profile categories, services and photos](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-business-profile-optimisation-categories-services-photos-2026) explains the fields; fill in the factual ones and leave the promotional ones empty.

## DPDP consent basics for enquiry forms

An enquiry form collects personal data, so the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is relevant to the firm. The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified on 14 November 2025. According to the SCC Online summary we consulted, the rules on notice, security safeguards and retention take effect eighteen months after publication, around mid-May 2027. Confirm the dates with your adviser and build to the standard now.

Per that summary, the notice must be clear, in simple language and separate from other information, stating the data collected, the purpose, the fiduciary's contact details, and how to withdraw consent or raise a grievance. For a CA firm's form:

- place a short notice directly above the submit button: what is collected, that it is used to respond to the enquiry, and a link to the full privacy notice;
- use an unticked checkbox for anything beyond replying, such as receiving professional updates, and record the date and time of consent;
- apply the safeguards the rules describe (encryption, access controls, logging, backups) to the form database and the document area, and load no advertising or remarketing tags.

## Build options, indicative costs and timelines

These are indicative ranges for Pune in late 2026, not a quotation.

| Option | What it includes | Indicative cost | Timeline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Template-based site | 6-10 pages on a CMS theme, partner profiles, contact form | ₹25,000 to ₹60,000 | 2 to 3 weeks |
| Custom-designed CMS site | Custom design, service and industry pages, knowledge section, multiple offices, consent logging | ₹75,000 to ₹2,00,000 | 5 to 8 weeks |
| Site with client document area | The above plus secure client login, per-client folders, staff roles, access logs | ₹2,00,000 to ₹6,00,000 | 10 to 16 weeks |

Typically included: design, development, mobile layouts, basic on-page SEO, forms, SSL and CMS training. Typically excluded: domain and hosting renewals, photography, article writing, the firm's own ethics review, and third-party security testing of the document area. Running costs for hosting, backups, updates and support are indicatively ₹15,000 to ₹60,000 a year. See our [website pricing](/pricing/websites) page for current packages.

Content approval is the slowest part: budget two rounds of partner review.

### A worked example (illustrative)

This is an illustration, not a client case. A five-partner firm with a head office in Pune and a branch in Pimpri-Chinchwad replaces a 2019 site that has a "why choose us" block, a client logo strip and a testimonial slider. In the rebuild:

- the three blocks go. A "Clients" page lists, as text, only companies that gave written permission, with name only for audit clients;
- each partner gets a profile with year of qualification, areas of experience and membership number;
- the firm links to its existing practice management login instead of building a document store;
- the budget falls in the middle band, with launch in seven weeks, two of them partner review.

## Pre-launch checklist

- Firm name, FRN, addresses and partner details match ICAI records (clause 3.3.21).
- No fees, testimonials, star ratings, catch phrases, superlatives or comparisons anywhere, including meta descriptions and image alt text.
- Client names shown only with written permission; name only for exclusive services.
- No banner ads, pop-ups or advertising scripts; outbound links limited to ICAI, government, regulators and professional bodies.
- Enquiry form has a notice, unticked consent boxes and spam protection.
- Document area tested: one client cannot see another's files, and staff use two-factor login.
- One partner has signed off every page against the current Chapter 3, with the review date recorded.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a CA firm have a website in India?

Yes. Clause 3.3.1 of the Council Guidelines for Advertisement in ICAI's Code of Ethics says chartered accountants, their firms and ICAI-registered networks are free to create their own website, and no standard format is prescribed. The content must stay within the permitted particulars and must not amount to soliciting clients or professional work.

### Can a chartered accountant show client names on the website?

Under the revised Code applicable from 1 April 2026, a firm may mention the name of a client and the nature of the assignment with the client's permission. For services exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, such as audit, only the client name may be mentioned. Fees charged cannot be shown, and testimonials remain prohibited.

### Are testimonials and Google reviews allowed on a CA firm website?

No. The Guidelines say a write-up should not contain testimonials or endorsements concerning members or the fees charged. Reviews that clients post on Google on their own are outside the firm's control, but the firm should not solicit them or republish them on its website.

### Can CA firms run Google Ads or do SEO?

The Code permits blogs, articles and professional updates on the website, so search visibility earned through useful content fits within the rules. It also says members must not issue any advertisement that solicits people to visit their website and bars banner advertising on the site. Whether paid search ads are allowed for non-exclusive services after the 2026 revision is not settled in the text, so confirm with ICAI's Ethical Standards Board first.

### How much does a CA firm website cost in Pune?

As an indicative range, a template-based site costs about ₹25,000 to ₹60,000, a custom-designed CMS site about ₹75,000 to ₹2,00,000, and a site with a secure client document area about ₹2,00,000 to ₹6,00,000. Annual running costs for hosting, updates and support are roughly ₹15,000 to ₹60,000.
